stances.claim: Endo / 5-5-5 -- hiring for exactly five months to evade the six-month regularization threshold -- is definitely illegal and subversive of public interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: unambiguous condemnation of the most abusive practice

stances.claim: Labor-only contracting is illegal: the contractor is deemed merely an agent of the principal, making the principal solidarily liable for all rightful worker claims.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal statement from Sasan and Valencia

stances.claim: Legal job-contracting is unquestionably valid: independent business, substantial capital or investment, control only over results, and full labor-standard protection for contractual employees.
The President and DOLE do not have the power to prohibit legitimate job-contracting or mandate only direct hiring -- they can only implement, not modify, expand, or repeal the Labor Code.
stances.rhetorical_move: separation-of-powers limitation on executive labor regulation

stances.claim: Article 239 of the Revised Penal Code penalizes any public officer who encroaches upon legislative power by making rules beyond the scope of authority or suspending a law.
If labor groups want all subcontracting prohibited, they should look to Congress, not the executive, for relief.

Article 239 of the Revised Penal Code -- penalizing public officers who encroach on legislative power -- cited as a criminal backstop against executive overreach in labor regulation.
Sasan v. NLRC (2008) as the governing case for both the illegal labor-only contracting test and the legal job-contracting three-pronged test.

one_paragraph_summary: On Labor Day, President Duterte signed Executive Order No. 51 protecting the right to security of tenure and prohibiting contracting used to circumvent that right -- but organized labor was disappointed because the EO did not end all subcontracting or mandate only direct hiring. Duterte defended his restraint frankly: 'You're asking me to violate the law. What if I am impeached?' Spokesperson Roque added that the prohibition could only be expanded by legislation. Panganiban uses this as a teachable moment on the legal/illegal divide. On the illegal side: endo/5-5-5 -- hiring for exactly five months to evade the six-month regularization threshold -- is definitively illegal and subversive of public interest; so is labor-only contracting, where the contractor merely supplies workers without substantial capital (below P5 million per DOLE DO 174), without tools or supervision, and the workers perform activities directly related to the principal's main business -- making the contractor a mere agent and the principal solidarily liable for all worker claims (Sasan v. NLRC, October 17, 2008; Valencia v. Classique Vinyl, January 30, 2017). On the legal side: job-contracting is unquestionably valid under the Sasan three-prong test -- (1) independent business under contractor control except for results, (2) substantial capital or investment, (3) agreement ensuring contractual employees' full labor and occupational safety rights. Fixed-term, project, and seasonal employment are also allowed. The President and DOLE may only implement the Labor Code, not modify or repeal it -- Article 239 of the Revised Penal Code penalizes public officers who encroach on legislative power by making rules beyond their authority. The column closes by redirecting organized labor: for the prohibition of all contracting and a mandate of direct-only hiring, look to Congress, not the executive.
